content:
I just turned 34! 🎂 I LEARNT A LOT this year... Here are 3 things that might help ya 👇🏾

🔋 1. Energy is the foundational currency of life. 

I recently interviewed the leading mitochondria expert and the neuroscientist who popularised the idea of our finite daily "body budget." 

In this very noisy season of my life, every distraction, opportunity (they look the same), or social media scroll presents a temptation to spend my energy unproductively and unintentionally.

Once I fully appreciated that energy is THE finite biological currency - the centre point of my influence - determining everything I care about (family, business, health) - I became much more careful about where I placed my thoughts, as my thoughts direct my energy and I became much more diligent about what I say YES to!

After all, the biggest risk to a GREAT idea is energy wasted on lots of GOOD ones!

Becoming a master of "NO" is mission-critical and it's a skill the greatest entrepreneurs I've ever met all seem to have.

(Plus, I hope to become a dad soon, so I better get good at saying NO before a kid arrives!)

⏰ 2. The magical power of long-term thinking. 

A single 39-year-old friend recently told me, "Steven, I absolutely do NOT want to be dating this time next year." 

Unknowingly, when he said this, his goal shifted from "find someone to love" to "find the best person available before the 12-month clock runs out." - two very different goals.

He'll likely rush, overlook red flags, and repeat his cycle. 

This is the paradox of short-term thinking: we often waste time trying to save time. 

Often, the SLOW way is the FAST way, because the slow way is the ONLY way. 

A thought experiment: if I gave you unlimited bricks and 10 seconds to build a tower, you'd stack them vertically, only for a gust of wind to knock it down. 

If I gave you 1 year, you'd lay them horizontally, making a wide boring foundation and build a tower ten times taller that is built to last!

The point here is that, the time horizon you apply will change your decisions today, and today's decisions change your outcomes tomorrow.

This is long-term thinking - the ultimate (but increasingly rare) life-hack, in a world where people think about their life in 5 year segments.

By thinking in decades instead, my decisions across every area of my life I care about, have changed drastically.

So, I now endeavour to be impatient with the short term (move as fast as I can today), and patient with the long term (my long term goals).

The Romans has a phrase for this: festina lente (Make haste... slowly).

🎉 3. Catch the good old days in the act. 

The tragedy of "the good old days" is we rarely notice them while we're in them. We have to call them out! 

At 34, I'm doing work I love, surrounded by people I love. 

I am in the middle of the good old days. 

Thank you so much for the birthday messages! ❤️ 😊

If you're great at what you do, but nobody knows, that's a "you" problem.

The market isn't going to discover you because you deserve it.

But, of course, someone half as talented is posting their work, explaining what they know, showing results, asking for the business, and getting paid.

Being uncomfortable with self-promotion is expensive.

But you don't need to become obnoxious.

You do need to get good at three things:

1. Show your work.

Talk about what you're building, what you're learning, what worked, and what failed. Be open, honest, and helpful.

2. Make your value extremely obvious.

Explain the problem you solve and show the result. Make it simple. A 6th-grader should be able to understand it.

3. Repeat yourself daily.

You are significantly more tired of your message than everyone else is. Most people missed it, forgot it, or are new to your world. Repeat!

People can't buy work they don't know exists.

And if you're building a one-person business, nobody else is coming to create that attention for you.

You have to learn how to get attention, earn trust, make good decisions, and turn your skills into income without spending your entire life doing it.

author: Richard Branson
authorInfo: Founder at Virgin Group
content:
How do you process failure, and move on from it? 

My answer is quite simple: learn the lesson, then move on. I’ve realised that dwelling on failure rarely makes the next idea any better.

A lesser-known example of mine was the launch of Event magazine. It was our version of a “what’s on" magazine that we launched in the early 1980s. The logic seemed sound: we were already an entertainment business, so a culture magazine felt like a natural extension. 

But it came up against Time Out, which was already proving extremely successful, and Event simply couldn’t compete. We really thought we had spotted a great opportunity, but it just didn’t work. We quickly shut it down and learnt a very important lesson: Always protect the wider brand from one company’s failure. Then we moved on. 

My mum used to say, “Don’t cry over spilt milk”, and that has always stayed with me. 

Of course, you will feel deflated and, to be honest, an immense amount of stress. Digging deep into it won’t make that any easier. Work out what went wrong and write down what you’ve learnt (this part is important). Then put your energy into what comes next.

As I’ve always said: Business opportunities are like buses, there’s always another one coming. Just make sure you’re not looking in the rearview mirror.

Most entrepreneurs try to build a business first and then cram their life around it.

I think that's a mistake.

Before you build anything, you should decide what your business is going to make possible in your life.

Here are some important questions to think through:

How many hours do you want to work?
How much income is actually enough?
Do you want weekends protected?
Do you want employees?
Do you want meetings?
Do you want to travel?

Those answers should help shape the business model that you eventually choose.

Because the answers affect what you sell, how you price it, how much complexity you install, and what kinds of customers you avoid.

You can build a "great" business and still build the wrong one for the life you want to live.

So define your life first.
Then build the business that supports it.

That was how I approached my one-person business, and it forced me to get excellent at a handful of skills:

Choosing the best work for me.
Keeping everything overly simple.
Protecting my time (especially weekends).
Creating predictable income with automation.
And growing without adding any complexity.

content:
There are three important decisions that have an outsized impact on your life.

1. Who you marry

Who you marry isn't only about the best of times.

It's also about your support system in the most difficult times.

All in all, probably the most important decision you can make.

2. Where you live

The place you call home should align with your energy and the type of community you want to build.

Love that city chaos? Get in there.
Need that quiet country serenity? Find it.
Need both? Try your best to split your time.

3. How you earn a living

There's nothing worse than building a business that you hate working in.

A business can make you rich and still be a terrible business for you.

If it requires 80-hour weeks, some giant team you never wanted, or spending a ton of your time doing work you hate, money doesn't magically make that a good deal.

I always wanted something different.

A business that earned extremely well, stayed simple, and left me enough time and energy for the rest of my life.

The first 30 minutes after waking up could shape your entire day.

By the time you’re exhausted at night, your brain may be operating very differently.

Andrew Huberman put it simply: “Don’t say things tired.”

When we’re exhausted, our impulse control gets worse. The message you want to send, the argument you want to have or the decision that suddenly feels urgent can look completely different after some sleep.

That was one of many moments in this conversation that made me realise how much is happening inside our brains and bodies without us really understanding it.

Andrew is a neuroscientist and professor at Stanford, and what I value about speaking to him is that he goes beyond the simple health headlines and explains what is actually happening underneath them.

Cortisol isn’t simply “bad”. Ozempic isn’t only about weight loss. And some of the smallest things we do every day can have a surprisingly large effect on how we sleep, think and feel.

We covered things like:

- The 10 protocols to become the healthiest version of yourself
- When cortisol is actually good for you
- The eye movement trick that could help you fall asleep
- A neuroscientist’s perspective on God and religion
- The simple trick that can lower blood sugar spikes

One thing that really stayed with me was just how adaptable our brains are.

Andrew explained that repeatedly doing things you don’t want to do can physically change an area of the brain associated with tenacity. It made me look differently at the workout I want to skip, the difficult conversation I’m avoiding and those moments where choosing discomfort might actually prepare me for whatever comes next.

That’s why I enjoy conversations with Andrew. You leave with practical things you can use immediately but also ideas that change how you think about your own behaviour.

This conversation definitely did that for me.

I think it might for you too.

"Rise and grind."
"I'll sleep when I'm dead."

Lol. OK.

There's nothing wrong with hard work. I love working hard.

Monday was Tim Cook's last day as CEO at Apple.

I first met Tim in 2014 and I've been fortunate to call him a mentor and friend ever since. I want to share something about him that I've found remarkable.

He's the best example I've seen of an old Zen saying:

"What do you do before enlightenment? Chop wood, carry water. What do you do after enlightenment? Chop wood, carry water."

When we met, I was just starting my career in finance. I was getting to the gym at 4:45am so I could get to the office by 6:30. Tim happened to be one of a tiny group of others who showed up every morning at that early hour.

For the first six months, I had no idea who he was. I wasn't in tech and, having played college sports, I was frankly quite oblivious to the entire business world.

I remember being shocked after someone told me that the guy I was talking to in the mornings was the CEO of Apple.

For two reasons:

1. He had zero pretension about him. I never would have known how important or powerful he was.

2. He was already successful. Why the hell was he waking up at 4am to go to the gym?

Now, to be fair, in 2014, there were still questions about whether he was going to be an impactful successor to the legend that was Steve Jobs. A lot of people weren't sure he would be able to fill those enormous shoes.

But a few years later, he was still there. He had created a trillion dollars of value. People were calling him one of the best CEOs in the world. And he was still showing up at 4:45am. Still doing the same thing.

Chop wood, carry water.

As you start to experience success, notoriety, and achievement, it’s easy to lose sight of the work that got you those things in the first place. It’s easy to get distracted by results. By recognition. By the illusion that success somehow exempts you from the basics.

It doesn’t.

The outcomes may change. The titles may change. The scale may change. But the work doesn’t.

Chopping wood and carrying water means showing up when no one is watching. Doing the boring work well. Being reliable. Executing consistently. Returning to fundamentals even when you think you’re above them. Especially then.

Tim has been an example of that in my life. I'm grateful for having been able to see it up close.

And I also know that whatever he does next, the same thing will apply.

Chop wood, carry water.

author: Marcela González Morales
authorInfo: Auditoría y mejora de procesos con enfoque práctico y orientado a resultados
content:
“Eso lo maneja Calidad.”

Hay una frase que es muy común al interior de las organizaciones, pero que hacé más ruido aún durante una auditoría, cuando el auditor pregunta por un indicador y el responsable responde que lo tiene Calidad.
 
Pregunta por los riesgos del proceso y nuevamente: Eso lo maneja Calidad.
Pregunta cómo se hace seguimiento al desempeño, qué acciones se han tomado o dónde están determinadas ciertas actividades… y la respuesta vuelve a ser la misma.
 
¿Qué está pasando aquí?
 
Que posiblemente tenemos un sistema de gestión que está siendo administrado por Calidad, pero no necesariamente gestionado por quienes son responsables de los procesos.
 
Y son cosas muy diferentes.  Calidad puede acompañar. El proceso debe ser gestionado por su responsable.
 
El responsable de Calidad puede orientar metodologías, facilitar herramientas, consolidar información, hacer seguimiento al sistema, acompañar a los procesos y promover la mejora.
 
Pero quien lidera un proceso debería poder explicar, como mínimo:
🔹 ¿Cuál es el propósito de su proceso?
🔹 ¿Cuáles son sus principales riesgos y controles?
🔹 ¿Qué resultados debe alcanzar?
🔹 ¿Cómo sabe si está funcionando?
🔹 ¿Qué problemas ha identificado?
🔹 ¿Qué decisiones o mejoras ha implementado?
🔹 ¿Qué evidencias puede demostrar?

Si para responder estas preguntas siempre necesitamos acudir a Calidad, estamos ante un riesgo importante:  el sistema de gestión funciona… pero funciona depende exclusivamente de Calidad.
 
Los responsables terminan viendo los indicadores como “los indicadores de Calidad”, los riesgos como “la matriz que hizo Calidad”, las auditorías como “algo que revisa Calidad” y las acciones de mejora como “tareas que pidió Calidad”.
 
Y entonces el sistema deja de ser una herramienta para gestionar la organización y se convierte en un sistema paralelo que alguien debe mantener.
 
Una auditoría puede ayudarnos a detectar esto, pregúntate: 
“¿Cómo está funcionando mi proceso respecto al Sistema de Gestión?”
 
Un proceso realmente maduro no depende de que alguien de Calidad esté al lado para explicar y sus resultados y funcionamiento.
 
El responsable conoce su proceso, conoce sus resultados, conoce sus problemas, y  participa en sus decisiones y mejoras.
 
Calidad no es quien responde por todos los procesos, es quien ayuda a que cada proceso tenga la capacidad de responder por sí mismo.
 
La calidad no es responsabilidad de Calidad, es responsabilidad de quienes hacen y gestionan los procesos.
 
Si mañana Calidad no estuviera en la reunión, ¿podrías explicar cómo está funcionando tu proceso?

There is a side of corporate layoffs that people rarely talk about on here, and it isn't the financial stress—it’s the silence.

When you spend years in the trenches with a team, sharing late nights, venting sessions and happy hours, tight deadlines, and daily life, you naturally begin to view those colleagues as friends and for me in many cases, a trusted work family. You assume that the bond exists outside of an org chart...

Then, the layoff happens. Your laptop goes dark. And suddenly, some of the colleagues you trusted most, the people you talked to every day for years completely disappear.
No text. No email. No "Are you doing okay?"

It is a uniquely isolating experience and difficult to discern what was really vs fantasy. It makes you look back and question the validity of years of hard work and shared victories. The silence feels personal, even when you logically know it might just be corporate awkwardness, survivor's guilt, or fear. 

But here is the lesson I am taking away from the quiet: 
Workplace proximity is not the same as genuine community. A layoff will instantly filter your network, showing you exactly who was a true connection and who was just a desk neighbor. It hurts to realize the difference, but it is also a powerful form of clarity.

To anyone else navigating the heavy silence of a sudden career transition: you are not invisible, and your worth wasn’t tied to that building. We keep moving forward. And for everyone that has reached out, THANK YOU. You have given me hope and I can't be more grateful for your outreach.❤️

author: Sahil Bloom
authorInfo: NYT Bestselling Author | Entrepreneur | Investor
content:
A two-decade-old column changed how I see time.

(I used to think I was behind.)

In the year 2000, a man wrote to the Dear Abby advice column.

He said, "I'm a 36-year-old college dropout. My lifelong dream was to be a doctor. I have a good job selling pharmaceutical supplies, but my heart is still in medicine. If I go back to college, get my degree, go to medical school, do my internship, and finally start practicing, it'll take me seven years. In seven years, I'll be 43 years old. What do you think?"

Dear Abby's response: "And how old will you be in seven years if you don't go to medical school?"

Let that sink in.

When I read that, I flashed back to every single version of "it's too late" I've ever told myself.

Every story about being off track, behind, or lost.

Back to my late 20s when I felt like a failure while watching people post about their startup's funding round, their promotion, their Forbes 30 under 30 accolade.

All those times I longed for someone to come tap me in, tell me I was on track, tell me I was worthy.

But here's what it took me years to understand.

The timeline in my head was entirely invented.

My own creation, an abstraction so far removed from reality it didn't even resemble the real thing anymore.

We built these timelines from a young age.

We look at the world, scroll social media, and sketch out a map of how life is supposed to go.

What we should have done by 25, 35, and why we can't possibly start now.

We tie ourselves in knots.

We know what we really want, but we're too afraid to go all in because going all in means exposing yourself to real failure, being completely naked.

But here's the harsh truth Dear Abby nailed.

Time doesn't care about you.

It's moving with or without you, whether you act or not, whether you live the way you want or not.

Time is just going to pass.

And the research backs this up.

A Cornell University study found something powerful.

We regret our actions in the short term, but in the long term, we regret inaction.
It's never the things we did that haunt us, it's the things we didn't do.

Here's my question to you: How often do we all sit around waiting for someone else to come tap us into our own life?

To give us permission to go and do the thing we want to do.

The real lesson here is recognizing you don't need any of that.

You don't need permission. You don't need a Dear Abby column. You don't 
need this video.

You need to just tap yourself in.

You get to choose.

You're not late, you're not early, you're exactly where your life has led you to be.

And you get to decide where you go from here.

That thing you want to do, how old will you be in seven years if you don't?

——

author: Arianna Huffington
authorInfo: Founder and CEO at Thrive Global | Passionate about Health and AI
content:
AI models have jumped containment but our collective conversation about AI is far too contained. This week another set of frontier AI models was set for release, with announcements for the upcoming launch of OpenAI’s Astra and Anthropic’s Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1.
 
In a post on X about Astra, Sam Altman wrote about how “the world will need aligned AI” and that “an iterative loop where society and this technology evolve together is what will lead to the highest chance of getting this right.” 

He talks about society, but what is society? Society consists not just of institutions but individuals. For society to evolve, individuals have to evolve, but what are we asking of ourselves? That’s the part of the AI conversation we never get to.
 
“Evolve together” seems to mostly mean humans accommodating themselves to AI as it gets better and better. But why are we assuming machines can keep getting better but humans can't? 

As we work toward recursive self-improvement in machines, we seem to have lost sight of the recursive self-improvement that’s built into our humanity. We’re born to evolve — not as a metaphor or a self-help slogan, but as an imperative built into our design.
 
And yet as the AI models become more powerful, the humans in the equation seem to become less powerful and have less agency. Of course safety is important, but it’s not the only part of the conversation that matters. Thriving is about more than just avoiding the worst-case scenario.
 
“AI is getting extremely capable,” Altman wrote. But as AI is becoming more capable, we need just as much focus on how humans can become more capable. Evolving together has to mean more than just watching AI become more powerful and accommodating ourselves to it. 

Society evolves only when its members evolve.
